query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Thermo-mechanical processing can improve the strength-ductility balance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
generation.intervention: Thermo-mechanical processing, such as cold rolling with a thickness reduction of 8%
generation.conditions: Room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 700°C
generation.structural_mediator: Refined microstructure with increased dislocation density and grain refinement
generation.mechanism: Strain hardening and grain boundary strengthening
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength-ductility balance, with increased proof stress and fracture stress while maintaining decent ductility
generation.baseline: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6% at room temperature
generation.boundary: Temperature range up to 700°C, strain rate, and processing parameters
generation.uncertainty: Optimal thermo-mechanical processing parameters, long-term stability, and potential degradation mechanisms

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing and microstructural characterization of as-cast and thermo-mechanically processed AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermo-mechanical processing does not result in improved strength-ductility balance, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high entropy alloys (HEAs), offer a new paradigm in structural alloy design and development owing to their appealing physical and mechanical properties such as high fracture toughness, good wear and fatigue resistance, high strength and good elevated temperature properties. Several HEA systems have been reported with a single-phase face center cubic (FCC) or body center cubic (BCC) structure. To concurrently achieve good ductility of FCC HEAs along with high strength of BCC HEAs, eutectic high entropy alloys (EHEAs) have recently been developed to overcome the limitations of single-phase HEAs. EHEAs typically consist of a mixture of two solid-solution phases in the form of lamellae or rod-like dispersions in a matrix. To date, several EHEAs have been reported with excellent combination of high strength and ductility including CoFeNi1.4VMo, Co2.0Mo0.8Ni2.0VW0.8, CoFeNi2.0V0.5Nb0.75, CoCrFeNiTa0.4, CoCrFeNiNb0.65, Fe20Co20Ni41Al19, CoCrFeNiTax, AlCoCrFeNbxNi, AlCoCrFeNiZrx, and AlCoCrFeNix.
